extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/practitioners admitted to practice before the USPTO and counsel/officials handling USPTO reciprocal discipline (OED, USPTO Director)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing imposition of reciprocal discipline by the USPTO under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24, including the Selling presumption, the respondent's burdens to defeat reciprocal discipline, requirements for nunc pro tunc imposition, and duties under § 11.58 during suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal presumption of reciprocal discipline (Selling presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: State-imposed discipline creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline by the USPTO is proper (Selling v. Radford).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO treats the state disciplinary adjudication as presumptively valid; the Director is not sitting as a court of review to reweigh the state court's findings. A respondent must overcome this presumption by meeting the narrow tests set out in 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) and relevant case law (e.g., Selling, In re Kramer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on respondent to defeat reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent bears the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the defenses under Selling applies and thus precludes imposition of reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts and the USPTO require clear and convincing evidence that a genuine issue of material fact exists regarding one of the listed grounds (due process deprivation, infirmity of proof, grave injustice, or that the practitioner was not publicly disciplined). The standard is narrow; mere disagreement with state findings is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) — due process deprivation (i)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid reciprocal discipline, practitioner must clearly and convincingly show a genuine issue of material fact that the proceeding elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a narrow defense: the deficiency must be so severe (notice/opportunity-to-be-heard failure) that due process was denied. General complaints about procedure that do not rise to that level will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) — infirmity of proof (ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent reciprocal discipline, practitioner must clearly and convincingly show a genuine issue of material fact that there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense requires demonstrating that the evidentiary basis for the state finding is so weak or flawed that the USPTO could not accept it as final. The USPTO will not reweigh evidence lightly; the infirmity must be substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) — grave injustice (iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must clearly and convincingly show a genuine issue of material fact that imposition of identical discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grave injustice inquiry focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct—that the state's sanction was so ill-fitted that imposing it federally would be unjust. It does not concern timing (e.g., seeking nunc pro tunc relief); the respondent must argue that the underlying sanction itself was inappropriate. Prior voluntary stipulations by respondent undercut this claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1) — public discipline status argument (iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner may argue that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified to avoid imposing identical discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows a challenge based on the form or existence of public discipline; the respondent still must show a genuine issue of material fact by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of identical discipline absent successful defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification imposed by the state unless the practitioner meets one of the § 11.24(d)(1) defenses by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, unless the respondent clears the high bar for one of the defenses, the federal sanction mirrors the state sanction (same type and terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim to prevent reciprocal discipline (or to obtain a different result) must be supported by clear and convincing evidence of a genuine issue of material fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a higher-than-preponderance but lower-than-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard; courts and the USPTO apply it strictly in reciprocal-discipline contexts. The respondent must produce strong, credible evidence to overcome the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nunc pro tunc (§ 11.24(f)) eligibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be imposed nunc pro tunc only if the practitioner promptly notified the OED Director of the out-of-jurisdiction discipline and establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner voluntarily ceased all activities related to practice before the Office and complied with all provisions of § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two core requirements: (1) prompt notice to OED of the sanction imposed elsewhere; (2) proof (clear and convincing) that the practitioner stopped all USPTO-related practice voluntarily and complied fully with § 11.58 (client notifications, withdrawals, etc.). The effective date of nunc pro tunc relief is the date the practitioner ceased practice and complied with § 11.58. Substantial (but not complete) compliance is insufficient—full compliance is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties during suspension and for nunc pro tunc eligibility (§ 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must comply with the duties enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58, including promptly notifying clients of suspension, filing notices of withdrawal for pending matters where required, and ceasing all activities related to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples referenced: § 11.58(b)(1)(ii) (notify clients of suspension) and § 11.58(b)(1)(i) (file notice of withdrawal for pending trademark applications). Failure to perform these duties undermines claims of voluntary cessation and eligibility for nunc pro tunc relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of regulatory duties is not a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney's ignorance of the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 11.1 et seq. (including § 11.24 and § 11.58) is not an excuse for failing to comply and will not excuse noncompliance in disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities emphasize that lawyers are expected to know and comply with ethical and procedural duties; courts routinely reject ignorance as a defense in similar contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice analysis: focus on proportionality of sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: To show grave injustice, the inquiry focuses on whether the sanction imposed by the original jurisdiction was within the appropriate range given the misconduct—i.e., whether the punishment 'fits' the misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples show grave injustice is not established where the state sanction is within the typical range for the offense; voluntary stipulations to discipline undercut a grave injustice claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for USPTO/OED notices and responses
rubrics_metrics.description: When the OED Director files a Complaint for Reciprocal Discipline, the USPTO issues a Notice and Order giving the respondent a specified time (e.g., 40 days) to respond with all information that would establish a genuine issue of material fact under § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must timely file a response addressing the § 11.24(d)(1) defenses; failure to raise and support defenses within procedural timeframes undermines relief. The Order illustrates sequences: Complaint mailed, Notice and Order served, respondent's response, OED reply, Director's orders for further submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation enforcement procedure (Order-to-Show-Cause process)
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED believes the respondent failed to comply with a provision of the Final Order during probation, OED shall (1) issue an Order to Show Cause, (2) send it to respondent’s last address of record, and (3) grant 15 days to respond; if noncompliance remains, OED delivers materials to USPTO Director and requests immediate suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets out steps for enforcement of probation terms—timely service, opportunity to respond, and escalation to the USPTO Director for disciplinary action. Any review by the respondent of a subsequent USPTO Director order will not stay the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and interagency notice obligations (§ 11.59 and Official Gazette)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must publish a Notice in the Official Gazette describing the suspension and reasons, and must give notice pursuant to § 11.59 to disciplinary enforcement agencies in states of admission, courts of admission, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity of discipline is mandatory: the notice describes the sanction, the factual basis (e.g., conflict of interest violations), and directs readers to OED's public reading room for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific disciplinary terms imposed (case-specific requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this Final Order the respondent is suspended from practice before the Office in trademark and non-patent law for two years (serve 60 days, remainder stayed during two-year probation), must take and pass the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination (MPRE) within specified time, and is placed on probation for two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the concrete sanctions and conditions the USPTO may (and did) impose when reciprocal discipline is upheld. They illustrate the types of identical sanctions the USPTO mirrors from state orders (suspension length, probation, testing requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on waivers under § 11.3(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Waivers of certain regulatory requirements (e.g., petition for reinstatement procedures under § 11.60(a)-(d) and § 11.60(g)) may be granted pursuant to § 11.3(a) but are limited to the facts of the particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any waiver of procedural or regulatory requirements is fact-specific and not a general entitlement; orders granting waivers expressly state that they are limited to case facts.
